quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on the vocabulary of twills: the rule, warp-faced and balanced twills, steep, S and Z, and pointed twills.

questions.q: What does the notation 2/1 tell you about one end of the twill?
options: The end is up for two picks and down for one
The end is down for two picks and up for one
questions.explain: The numbers are the lifting order of one end: up/down. 2/1 is two up, one down; 1/2 would be its weft-faced opposite.

questions.q: The twill diagonal runs at 45° when:
options: The step is one end per pick
The step is two ends per pick
questions.explain: Moving the lifting order one end to the right on each pick gives a 45° line. A step of two ends per pick steepens it to 63°.

questions.q: Which of these twills are warp-faced?
questions.explain: A warp-faced twill has more 'up' than 'down' in its lifting order, so mostly warp shows on the face: 2/1 and 3/1. 1/2 and 1/3 are their weft-faced backs.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill looks the same on both sides of the cloth.
questions.explain: Each end is up for two picks and down for two, so the face and back show equal warp and weft; the twill is balanced and reversible.

questions.q: If you turn a 3/1 twill cloth over, what do you see on the back?
questions.explain: Wherever warp is on the face, weft is on the back, so the proportions invert: 3/1 becomes 1/3 with the diagonal leaning the other way.

questions.q: Which description fits cavalry twill?
options: A steep 63° twill with a pronounced double ridge, built by advancing two ends per pick
A twill reversed on the draft to make points
A twill with the lifting order shifted to the left
questions.explain: Cavalry twill is a steep twill: the lifting order moves two ends per pick so the diagonal rises at 63°, and its double ridge is characteristic.

questions.q: An S twill is produced by:
options: Shifting the lifting order one end to the left on each pick
questions.explain: Shifting to the left gives an S twill; shifting to the right gives Z. Reversing the draft makes a pointed twill, not an S twill.

questions.q: A pointed twill is made by:
options: Reversing the draft at the end of the repeat so the twill line turns back on itself
questions.explain: Threading the ends 1-2-3-4-3-2 turns the diagonal back, forming chevrons warp-way. Advancing two ends per pick makes a steep twill.

questions.q: Which of these is an irregular twill?
questions.explain: An irregular twill has several up/down groups of different sizes in one lifting order, such as 2/1/1/2, but still shifts one end per pick. The others are regular twills with one up group and one down group.

questions.q: Twills interlace more often than plain weave and must therefore be set more openly.
questions.explain: The opposite: twills interlace less often than plain weave (floats of two or three), so they can be set denser, which the cover-factor divisors in Weaving Calculations 12 allow for.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Repeat sizes, twill angles, warp-face proportions and what changes when the step or direction changes.

questions.q: What is the repeat size of a 2/1 twill?
questions.explain: The repeat is the sum of the up and down numbers, 2 + 1 = 3, on both ends and picks. Six would be the repeat of 2/1/1/2.

questions.q: What is the repeat of the irregular twill 2/1/1/2?
questions.explain: Add all the groups: 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6 ends and 6 picks. Counting only the up groups (2 + 1 = 3) or the number of groups (4) are common slips.

questions.q: If the lifting order advances two ends per pick instead of one, the twill angle becomes approximately:
questions.explain: Two ends across for every pick up steepens the line to about 63°, the cavalry twill angle. A 27° line would come from advancing one end every two picks.

questions.q: Why can a twill be set denser than a plain weave of the same yarn?
options: Because the ends interlace less often, leaving more room for them to pack together
Because the diagonal pulls the ends apart
questions.explain: Fewer interlacings per inch mean fewer bends and less yarn crowding at each crossing, so more threads fit in the same width. This is reflected in the cover-factor divisors.

questions.q: What is the repeat, in ends, of a regular twill written 3/2/1/1?
questions.explain: The repeat is the sum of all the numbers: 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7 ends (and 7 picks).

questions.q: The lecture's 2/2 twill pointed on 6 ends is threaded:
questions.explain: The draft rises 1-2-3-4 and then falls 3-2, turning the twill line back; the next repeat starts at 1 again. A straight 1-2-3-4-5-6 draft would need 6 healds and give an ordinary twill.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill pointed on 6 ends needs 6 heald frames.
questions.explain: Only 4 healds are needed: ends 5 and 6 repeat the movements of ends 3 and 2, so they are drawn on the same healds (draft 1-2-3-4-3-2).

questions.q: What fraction of the face of a 3/1 twill is covered by warp?
questions.explain: Each end is up 3 picks out of 4, so 3 ÷ 4 = 75 % warp on the face. 66.7 % would be a 2/1 twill and 25 % a 1/3.

questions.q: Which of these twills is balanced?
questions.explain: Balanced means equal up and down in the lifting order, so 2/2 shows the same amount of warp and weft on both faces. 2/1 and 3/1 are warp-faced; 1/3 is weft-faced.

questions.q: Changing the shift from one end to the right to one end to the left on each pick changes:
options: The twill direction from Z to S
questions.explain: The direction of the shift fixes the slope of the diagonal: right gives Z, left gives S. Repeat, angle and face proportion are unchanged.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting repeats, filled squares, healds and floats for the twills in the lecture.

questions.q: How many squares are filled in one 3 × 3 repeat of a 2/1 twill?
questions.explain: Each of the 3 ends is up on 2 picks: 3 × 2 = 6 filled squares out of 9.

questions.q: How many squares are filled in one 4 × 4 repeat of a 2/2 twill?
questions.explain: Each of the 4 ends is up for 2 picks: 4 × 2 = 8 filled squares, exactly half of the 16.

questions.q: What percentage of the face of a 2/1 twill is warp? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: Up 2 of every 3 picks: 2 ÷ 3 = 0.667, i.e. 66.7 % warp on the face.

questions.q: What is the repeat of a regular twill written 2/2/1/1?
questions.explain: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 ends and 6 picks.

questions.q: How many heald frames does an ordinary (straight-drafted) 2/2 twill need?
questions.explain: The repeat has 4 ends, each with a different lifting order, so 4 frames with a straight draft 1-2-3-4.

questions.q: A twill is pointed on the draft 1-2-3-4-5-4-3-2. How many ends wide is the repeat?
questions.explain: Count the threading: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2 is 8 ends before the sequence restarts at 1; only 5 healds are used.

questions.q: The lecture's pointed 2/2 twill is drawn on 6 ends × 8 picks. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: Every end still follows a 2/2 order, up on half the picks: 6 × 8 = 48 squares, half filled = 24.

questions.q: An 8-end lifting order is advanced two ends to the right on each pick (steep twill). After how many picks does the pattern return to its starting position?
questions.explain: A shift of 2 ends per pick covers the 8-end repeat in 8 ÷ 2 = 4 picks, so the weave repeats on 8 ends × 4 picks.

questions.q: In a 2/1 twill pick 1 lifts ends 1 and 2. Which ends are lifted on pick 2?
questions.explain: Shift one end to the right: pick 2 lifts ends 2 and 3; pick 3 lifts ends 3 and 1. Lifting only end 3 would be the weft-faced 1/2 twill.

questions.q: What percentage of the face of the irregular twill 2/1/1/2 is warp?
questions.explain: Up groups total 2 + 1 = 3 picks out of a 6-pick repeat: 3 ÷ 6 = 50 %, so this irregular twill is balanced.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing and troubleshooting twills on the design table and the loom.

questions.q: A buyer wants a hard-wearing workwear drill with warp dominating the face. Which weave do you propose?
questions.explain: 3/1 is the classic drill: 75 % warp on the face gives a strong, smooth surface. 1/3 would put the weft on the face and 2/2 shows both equally.

questions.q: A blanket must look identical from either side. Which twill suits best?
questions.explain: A balanced 2/2 twill shows the same proportion of warp and weft on both faces, so it is reversible. Warp-faced twills show their weft-faced backs when turned.

questions.q: A plain-weave construction cannot be set as densely as the customer wants. What is the designer's first option?
options: Change to a twill, which interlaces less and accepts a denser sett
questions.explain: Twills interlace less often than plain weave, so the same yarn can be packed closer. A finer reed does not solve yarn jamming at the interlacings.

questions.q: An order for cavalry twill for riding breeches arrives. How does the designer obtain the characteristic steep ridge?
options: Shift the lifting order one end to the left
Advance the lifting order two ends per pick to give a 63° diagonal
Reverse the draft every four ends
questions.explain: The steep 63° angle and double ridge of cavalry twill come from a two-end step per pick. Shifting left only changes Z to S; reversing the draft makes points.

questions.q: A Z twill is running on the loom and the customer now wants an S twill. What is the simplest change?
options: Shift the lifting order one end to the left on each pick instead of to the right
questions.explain: The twill direction depends only on the direction of the shift, which is set in the lifting (peg) plan. No change to reed, yarn or frames is needed.

questions.q: A designer wants a chevron (zigzag) effect running warp-way in a 2/2 twill. What should be done?
questions.explain: Reversing the draft turns the twill line back on itself and forms points warp-way. A steep twill only changes the angle, not the direction.

questions.q: A loom has only 4 healds. Can it weave the lecture's 2/2 twill pointed on 6 ends?
options: Yes — ends 5 and 6 repeat the movements of ends 3 and 2, so the draft 1-2-3-4-3-2 uses 4 healds
Only if the picks per inch are reduced
questions.explain: Healds are set by distinct end movements, not by repeat width. The pointed draft brings ends 5 and 6 back onto healds 3 and 2.

questions.q: A sample of what should be a 3/1 twill shows mostly weft on the side being inspected. The most likely explanation is:
options: The inspector is looking at the back, which is a 1/3 twill
questions.explain: The back of a 3/1 twill is a 1/3 twill with 75 % weft on it. Turn the sample over before raising a complaint.

questions.q: Which of these twills can NOT be woven on a loom with only 4 healds and a straight draft?
questions.explain: 2/1/1/2 repeats on 6 ends with 6 different movements, so it needs 6 healds. The three regular twills need 3, 4 and 4 healds respectively.

questions.q: A 3/1 twill drill can be woven on an ordinary tappet loom.
questions.explain: It needs only 4 healds and a 4-pick repeat, comfortably within a tappet's 6–8 frames and 8-pick limit, which is why drills are so economical to weave.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the whole lecture: repeat logic, steep twills, pointed drafts and the mistakes students make most.

questions.q: A 2/2 twill is drawn on 8 ends × 8 picks. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: A 2/2 twill lifts half the ends on every pick, so half of the 64 squares are filled: 32. 48 would be a 3/1 twill and 16 a 1/3.

questions.q: How many heald frames does a regular twill written 3/2/1/2 need with a straight draft?
questions.explain: Repeat = 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8 ends, each moving differently, so 8 frames: the limit of a tappet.

questions.q: A student says a 2/1 twill repeats on 3 ends but only 2 picks. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — the pick repeat is always one less
The repeat is the same on ends and picks: 3 × 3, because the shift of one end per pick brings the pattern back after 3 picks
questions.explain: After 3 picks the lifting order has moved 3 ends, a full repeat, so the pattern returns to the start. For any regular twill with a one-end step, ends and picks repeat on the same number.

questions.q: The 6-end lifting order 2/1/1/2 is advanced two ends per pick to make a steep twill. On how many picks does the weave repeat?
questions.explain: A step of 2 covers the 6-end order in 6 ÷ 2 = 3 picks, so the repeat is 6 ends × 3 picks.

questions.q: A steep twill with a two-end step always repeats on the same number of picks as ends.
questions.explain: Only a one-end step gives a square repeat. With a two-end step the pattern returns after half as many picks (for an even repeat), e.g. 8 ends × 4 picks.

questions.q: Which draft correctly points a 2/2 twill on 6 ends?
questions.explain: The draft must climb through all four healds and then come back down without repeating the turning heald: 1-2-3-4-3-2. 1-2-3-4-1-2 is a straight draft that merely restarts.

questions.q: The pointed 2/2 twill is drawn on 6 ends × 8 picks. What is the true repeat in picks?
questions.explain: The lifting plan is still a 2/2 twill, which repeats on 4 picks; the 8-pick drawing shows two repeats to display the fabric effect. The 6-end width comes from the pointed draft.

questions.q: What percentage of the face of a 1/3 twill is warp?
questions.explain: Up 1 pick in 4: 1 ÷ 4 = 25 % warp, so 75 % weft on the face. It is the back of a 3/1.

questions.q: For a balanced 3/3 twill, which set of facts is correct?
questions.explain: Repeat = 3 + 3 = 6 ends and picks; six distinct movements need 6 healds; each end floats over (and under) 3 picks. The repeat is never the product of the numbers.

questions.q: Which twill has the longest floats and would therefore be most prone to snagging?
questions.explain: A 4/4 twill floats over 4 picks on each face. 3/1 floats over 3 on the face only; 2/2 and 2/1 float over 2. Longer floats mean more lustre but less firmness.
